To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

circulating tumor cells are detectable in ovarian cancer patients, that they may be used as prognostic markers and that the presence of disseminated tumor cells (DTC) is associated with poor survival in patients with advanced disease.
circulating tumor cells and tumor cell clusters can be detected in the circulation of ovarian cancer patients.
the presence of circulating tumor cells (CTC) and disseminated tumor cell (DTC) is associated with poor prognosis and survival of ovarian cancer patients.

the study of the molecular mechanisms underlying ovarian cancer development, progression, and metastasis.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of ovarian cancer and the development of novel targeted therapies for ovarian cancer.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of CTCs in the peripheral blood is a reliable and sensitive biomarker for ovarian cancer, with a high specificity for the disease and a low false positive rate.

there is a lack of evidence for a role of circulating tumor cells in the diagnosis of ovarian cancer, and there is a paucity of evidence to support their use as prognostic markers or as predictors of treatment response in ovarian cancer patients.

there is a need to develop a standardized protocol for the detection of circulating tumor cells in ovarian cancers, as well as to determine their clinical relevance and to evaluate the potential role of circulating tumor cells as a surrogate biomarker for ovarian cancer.

the data on circulating and disseminated tumor cell in ovarian cancer is limited.
the data on circulating and disseminated tumor cell (DTC) detection in patients with epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) is still scarce.
the data presented in this review support the idea that circulating tumor cells and disseminated tumor cell are important biomarkers for prognosis and response to therapy.

the presence of circulating tumor DNA is a promising marker for ovarian cancer detection.
